fields.title: Slyuda: New Dashboard Called Confusing
fields.summary: In beta feedback, the word 'confusing' appears in 19 out of 31 comments. Four weeks until release.
fields.decisionPrompt: What will you do in the remaining weeks, and what will you launch in the general release?
fields.brief/role: You are the product manager of Slyuda's analytics section.
fields.brief/company: Slyuda is a fictional company of 120 people that sells an inventory management system to mid-sized retail chains.
fields.brief/context: Six weeks ago, the redesigned dashboard was opened in beta to 240 clients. The old one was a wall of 22 tiles; the new one shows four key metrics, with the rest hidden under a 'More metrics' expander. In a survey of 47 responses, the word 'confusing' appears in 19 out of 31 free-text comments. The designer interprets this as 'we need to better explain the new layout' and suggests an onboarding tour. The head of development sees it as 'we hid what people actually need.' The general release is in four weeks.
fields.brief/objective: Decide what to launch in the general release.
fields.brief/constraints: Four weeks. One designer and two developers. The researcher is available for two days this week and none next week.
fields.brief/task: Choose what to do before the release and justify it.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: One word in feedback usually means several different problems
fields.learnTakeaway/body: 'Confusing' is not a diagnosis: it can hide 'I couldn't find it', 'you chose the wrong things', or 'I can't work with this'. Grouping identical words into categories and verifying each with behavior takes an hour and usually resolves two-thirds of the complaints. The remaining third usually belongs to a single segment, and that is where you actually change the layout.
fields.evidenceCards/0/title: What they wrote in the survey
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
The researcher conducted six half-hour sessions two weeks ago, before the survey closed.

Four users from single stores and small chains: all found their metrics in the expander within seconds and preferred the new layout. One said: 'it was confusing the first day, then it was fine.'

Two users from chains with 12 and 34 locations: both struggled. Their job is to compare a single metric across locations, but the new dashboard shows the company total, with location-specific data hidden three clicks deep. One said: 'this was made for someone who runs a single store.'

The researcher's conclusion: 'It looks like we don't have one problem, but two different ones.'
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Segment the feedback and look at chains
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Read the 19 comments as three distinct problems, spend the researcher's two days on multi-location chains, and define the release scope based on the results.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
Segmentation immediately changes the picture: 11 comments about 'where did it go' are about search, and behavior shows the issue is minor (the expander was opened by 78%, and time to first action dropped from 21 seconds to 9).
Five comments about 'why these four' are a different issue, and one of the four metrics is indeed dead: users interact with it in only 6% of sessions. It is replaced with turnover in a single day.
This leaves the third problem, which is the only real one: chains have a different job — comparing a metric across locations. All 14 rollback requests came from them, representing 40% of the section's revenue.
Two days of observations confirm that the layout doesn't work for them at all. You take the two-week delay and build the multi-location comparison, while launching as-is for single stores.
Trade-off: the release is delayed by two weeks, which had to be explained in two meetings.
fields.decisionOptions/1/label: Allow customizing the four key metrics
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: Spend eight days on customizable key metrics: this directly addresses the 'why these four' complaint and allows you to launch on time.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
The customization is released on time and resolves five out of nineteen comments — those about metric choice.
The side effect is predictable: the product no longer has a default opinion, and new clients see a screen they have to build first.
The core issue remains untouched: chains don't need a different set of numbers, they need to compare a single number across locations, which is still three clicks deep. All 14 rollback requests come from this segment.
After the release, the share of rollback requests grows along with the number of chains on the new dashboard.
Trade-off: you addressed the loudest of the three complaints rather than the most expensive one; however, the solution itself is reasonable and irreversible.
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: Interpret the feedback as a discoverability issue and spend three days on a tour highlighting the 'More metrics' expander.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
The tour is released in three days and changes almost nothing: 78% of users were already opening the expander, and the time to first action was half of what it was on the old dashboard.
People weren't lost — they either couldn't find the right breakdown or got the wrong layout.
After the release, rollback requests keep coming, all from the same segment.
A month later, the team is discussing a second tour.
Trade-off: the word 'confusing' was treated as a single problem and solved with training, even though behavior clearly showed that finding the expander was not the barrier.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Roll back the dashboard before release
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Nineteen comments out of thirty-one is a strong signal. Revert to the old version and rethink the redesign from scratch.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
The rollback silences the noise in a day, which is its only merit.
Along with it, confirmed improvements are discarded: time to first action of 9 seconds vs. 21, and 4.1 sessions per user vs. 3.6 for the same people.
The 12 positive comments and the four out of six observed users who preferred the new layout are also ignored.
A quarter later, the team returns to the same task with the same questions and not a single new fact.
Trade-off: the share of negative comments was taken as a verdict without segmentation; however, the rollback does eliminate risk before the peak season.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: The feature is described in isolation, without the pain point and the benefit on the other side
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: The chain from goal to behavior is incomplete, making it unclear why this needs to be done
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: Objects and their states are not defined before designing screens
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: The flow is designed only for the happy path: empty, error, and conflict states are ignored
fields.rubric/remediation/4/gap: Consistency and interface language are treated as cosmetic issues
